body.statement: For the isolated-bow baseline, \(P_{\sigma}(X_b=a,C_b=d,Y_b=1,S_b=1)=1/12\), \(P_{\sigma}(X_b=a,C_b=d,Y_b=0,S_b=1)=1/24\), and \(P_{\sigma}(S_b=1)=1/2\), so the two full selected observational laws agree. Under \(\operatorname{do}(X_b=0)\), the unselected outcome probabilities are \(9/16\) and \(7/16\), the selection normalizers are \(25/48\) and \(23/48\), the joint numerators at \(Y_b=C_b=1\) are \(9/25\) and \(7/23\), and the conditional effects are \(18/25\) and \(14/23\). However \(D_{\rho}=1/2\) in both models solely because \(C_b\) is an isolated fair root. This proposition is a vacuous-denominator regression baseline and supplies no evidence for generic denominator locking.
body.justification: Keeping the exact calculation visible prevents a structurally automatic denominator from being mistaken for evidence about informative conditioning.
body.gap: The baseline was previously used as support for denominator locking even though isolation makes the denominator equality automatic.
body.consumer: Certificate tests must classify this example as numerically valid but noninformative about the open graph-to-lock step.
body.proof_tex:
Fix \(\sigma\in\{-1,+1\}\) and \(a,d\in\{0,1\}\).  By the SCM factorization for the DAG \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{iso}}\) in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}isolated\mbox{-}bow\mbox{-}template}\),
\[
 P_{\sigma}(u,x,y,c,s)
 =P(u)P(c)P(x\mid u)P_{\sigma}(y\mid x,u)P(s\mid y).
\]
All displayed local probabilities in that definition are rational and lie strictly between zero and one.  In particular, the four possible outcome-mechanism values belong to
\[
 \left\{\frac{5}{16},\frac{7}{16},\frac{9}{16},\frac{11}{16}\right\}.
\]
Thus every cell needed below is positive, the conditioning operations are legitimate, and, together with Assumptions \(\mathrm{ass{:}binary\mbox{-}certificate\mbox{-}support}\) and \(\mathrm{ass{:}rational\mbox{-}interior\mbox{-}mechanisms}\), the two models have the stipulated positive rational binary support.

The treatment marginal is fair:
\[
 P(X_b=1)
 =\frac12\frac14+\frac12\frac34
 =\frac12,
 \qquad
 P(X_b=0)
 =\frac12\frac34+\frac12\frac14
 =\frac12.
\]
Bayes' formula may therefore be applied with a positive denominator, and it gives
\[
 P(U_b=1\mid X_b=0)
 =\frac{(1/2)(1/4)}{1/2}
 =\frac14=r_0^b,
 \qquad
 P(U_b=1\mid X_b=1)
 =\frac{(1/2)(3/4)}{1/2}
 =\frac34=r_1^b.
\]
Consequently, using the outcome mechanism from Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}isolated\mbox{-}bow\mbox{-}template}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 P_{\sigma}(Y_b=1\mid X_b=a)
 &=\sum_{u=0}^1
 \left\{\frac12+\frac{\sigma}{4}(u-r_a^b)\right\}
 P(U_b=u\mid X_b=a)\\
 &=\frac12+\frac{\sigma}{4}
 \left\{P(U_b=1\mid X_b=a)-r_a^b\right\}\\
 &=\frac12.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(C_b\) is an isolated fair root in \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{iso}}\), the factorization gives \(P(C_b=d)=1/2\) and makes \(C_b\) independent of \((X_b,Y_b,S_b)\).  Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
 P_{\sigma}(X_b=a,C_b=d,Y_b=1,S_b=1)
 &=P(X_b=a)P(C_b=d)
   P_{\sigma}(Y_b=1\mid X_b=a)P(S_b=1\mid Y_b=1)\\
 &=\frac12\frac12\frac12\frac23
 =\frac1{12},\\
 P_{\sigma}(X_b=a,C_b=d,Y_b=0,S_b=1)
 &=P(X_b=a)P(C_b=d)
   P_{\sigma}(Y_b=0\mid X_b=a)P(S_b=1\mid Y_b=0)\\
 &=\frac12\frac12\frac12\frac13
 =\frac1{24}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Summing these cells over the two values of \(a\) and the two values of \(d\) yields
\[
 P_{\sigma}(S_b=1)
 =4\left(\frac1{12}+\frac1{24}\right)
 =\frac12.
\]
It follows, cell by cell, that
\[
 P_{\sigma}(X_b=a,C_b=d,Y_b=y\mid S_b=1)
 =
 \begin{cases}
  1/6,&y=1,\\
  1/12,&y=0,
 \end{cases}
\]
which is independent of \(\sigma\).  Since the binary cells indexed by \((a,d,y)\) exhaust the observed sample space, the two full selected observational laws agree.

Now intervene to set \(X_b=0\).  The truncated SCM factorization leaves the fair root \(U_b\) unchanged.  Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
 p_{\sigma}
 &:=P_{\sigma}(Y_b=1\mid\operatorname{do}(X_b=0))\\
 &=\sum_{u=0}^1
 \left\{\frac12+\frac{\sigma}{4}\left(u-\frac14\right)\right\}P(U_b=u)\\
 &=\frac12+\frac{\sigma}{4}\left(\frac12-\frac14\right)
 =\frac12+\frac{\sigma}{16}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
 p_{+}=\frac9{16},
 \qquad
 p_{-}=\frac7{16}.
\]
The selection mechanism depends only on \(Y_b\), so its postintervention normalizer is
\[
\begin{aligned}
 Z_{\sigma}
 &:=P_{\sigma}(S_b=1\mid\operatorname{do}(X_b=0))\\
 &=\frac23p_{\sigma}+\frac13(1-p_{\sigma})
 =\frac{1+p_{\sigma}}3.
\end{aligned}
\]
It follows that
\[
 Z_{+}=\frac{25}{48},
 \qquad
 Z_{-}=\frac{23}{48},
\]
both of which are positive.  Take the terminal role state with \(\bar X=\{X_b\}\), \(\bar C=\{C_b\}\), outcome \(Y_b\), and assignments \(\bar x=0\), \(\bar c=1\).  Isolation of \(C_b\) is preserved by the intervention, and hence the selected terminal joint kernel is
\[
\begin{aligned}
 J_{\rho,\mathbf M_{\sigma}}(1,1;0)
 &=\frac{P_{\sigma}(Y_b=1,C_b=1,S_b=1
       \mid\operatorname{do}(X_b=0))}{Z_{\sigma}}\\
 &=\frac{p_{\sigma}(1/2)(2/3)}{Z_{\sigma}}
 =\frac{p_{\sigma}}{1+p_{\sigma}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitution gives the two claimed joint numerators,
\[
 J_{\rho,\mathbf M_{\mathrm{iso},+}}(1,1;0)=\frac9{25},
 \qquad
 J_{\rho,\mathbf M_{\mathrm{iso},-}}(1,1;0)=\frac7{23}.
\]
Moreover, the same isolation factorization gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 D_{\rho,\mathbf M_{\sigma}}(1;0)
 &=P_{\sigma}(C_b=1\mid\operatorname{do}(X_b=0),S_b=1)\\
 &=\frac{P(C_b=1)P_{\sigma}(S_b=1\mid\operatorname{do}(X_b=0))}{Z_{\sigma}}\\
 &=\frac{(1/2)Z_{\sigma}}{Z_{\sigma}}
 =\frac12.
\end{aligned}
\]
The division is valid because \(Z_{\sigma}>0\).  Normalizing the selected joint kernel by this denominator therefore yields
\[
 P_{\mathbf M_{\mathrm{iso},+}}(Y_b=1\mid
 \operatorname{do}(X_b=0),C_b=1,S_b=1)
 =\frac{9/25}{1/2}=\frac{18}{25},
\]
and
\[
 P_{\mathbf M_{\mathrm{iso},-}}(Y_b=1\mid
 \operatorname{do}(X_b=0),C_b=1,S_b=1)
 =\frac{7/23}{1/2}=\frac{14}{23}.
\]
Finally, the equation \(D_{\rho,\mathbf M_{\sigma}}(1;0)=1/2\) used only that \(C_b\) is an isolated fair root; it did not use cancellation between the sign-indexed outcome mechanisms.  Thus denominator equality is structurally automatic in this baseline, establishing precisely why the example is vacuous as evidence for generic denominator locking.
